title: Introduction and learning objectives
groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture on cancer causation and sets out its learning objectives.

title: Cancer evolution and susceptibility to mutations
groupedBecause: These subtopics establish how mutations produce evolving cancer clones and why some cells and individuals are more susceptible to that process.

title: Environmental cancer risks and their contribution to cancer incidence
groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how far environmental exposure explains cancer occurrence rather than inherited susceptibility or random mutation.

title: Infectious causes of cancer
groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections contribute to carcinogenesis, developing Burkitt lymphoma as a detailed example.

title: Mechanisms of DNA damage from environmental carcinogens
groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures damage DNA, showing how metabolic processing can determine their mutagenic effects.

title: Tumour initiation and promotion
groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutation-driven initiation from the conditions that promote tumour outgrowth and explain the experimental evidence for that distinction.

title: Tissue and developmental susceptibility, with a recap of carcinogenic mechanisms
groupedBecause: The explanation of tissue and life-stage susceptibility culminates in a recap emphasising that carcinogenic effects depend on the context in which exposures act.

title: Evidence linking human cancers to carcinogen exposure
groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence from human populations and samples can connect particular exposures with cancer development.

title: Experimental carcinogenicity testing and its limitations
groupedBecause: These subtopics assess how experimental tests detect carcinogenic potential and why their results may not capture cancer development in humans.

title: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
groupedBecause: This closing consolidates the lecture’s conclusions and frames their practical significance as decisions about risks and benefits.
